pages.x: For decades Gandhi's Congress party had led a mass movement of peaceful protest against British rule. In 1942 it told the British to quit India, and its leaders were jailed. By 1945 Britain, worn out by the Second World War, was ready to leave. The question was what would come after.

Muhammad Ali Jinnah, leader of the Muslim League, feared that Muslims, a quarter of India's people, would be at the mercy of a Hindu majority, and he demanded a separate homeland, Pakistan. When the League called a day of action in August 1946, riots in Calcutta killed thousands, and the violence spread.

The last viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, brought the handover forward by almost a year. At midnight on 15 August 1947 India became free, with Jawaharlal Nehru as its prime minister. He told the assembly that at the stroke of the midnight hour, while the world slept, India would awake to life and freedom. Pakistan had become free the day before.

The new border was drawn in five weeks by Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India, with old maps and census figures. It cut the provinces of Punjab and Bengal in two, and it was only made public two days after independence. Pakistan was born in two parts, 1,600 kilometres apart.

Hindus and Sikhs fled east out of Pakistan, and Muslims fled west out of India, in the largest mass migration in history. Trains arrived full of the dead. Mobs on every side murdered, burned and abducted, and somewhere between a few hundred thousand and two million people were killed.

Gandhi refused to celebrate. He walked through riot-torn villages and fasted in Delhi until the killing there stopped. On 30 January 1948 a Hindu nationalist who thought him too soft on Muslims shot him dead at a prayer meeting. Nehru told the nation that the light had gone out of their lives.

The princely state of Kashmir, mostly Muslim but ruled by a Hindu maharaja, joined India in October 1947 when raiders from Pakistan invaded. India and Pakistan fought their first war over it, and a ceasefire line in 1949 left it divided. They have fought over it again and again since.

Partition gave freedom to a fifth of humanity, and India became the world's largest democracy. But it left wounds that have never healed: the memories of 1947, the quarrel over Kashmir, and a rivalry between two nuclear-armed neighbours. In 1971 East Pakistan broke away to become Bangladesh.
